subsection: 7. Irish missionaries in Africa and Asia; case study: the Holy Ghost mission to Nigeria, 1945–1966

notes.b: Ireland sent Catholic missionaries to Africa and Asia out of proportion to its population, and this effort was given a national meaning.
points: Ireland had a large body of Catholic priests and religious for its population, and seminaries such as St Patrick’s College, Maynooth, trained many of them for overseas work.
The phrase Ireland’s spiritual empire described the reach of Irish missionaries across Africa and Asia, and it gave missionary work a national identity.
The Maynooth Mission to China was founded in 1916 to send Irish priests to China.
The Missionary Society of St Patrick, founded at Kiltegan, County Wicklow, in 1932, sent priests to Nigeria and other African countries.
The Society of African Missions and the Holy Ghost Fathers, called Spiritans, were other Irish-based societies working in Africa.
Irish parishes raised money through collections, missionary magazines and mission exhibitions, which linked congregations at home with the work abroad.

notes.b: Edward Galvin was a Maynooth Mission priest and bishop who worked in China during the upheavals of the 1930s and 1940s.
points: Edward Galvin was a Maynooth-trained priest who joined the Maynooth Mission to China, and he was among its leading founders and early members.
He worked in central China, where the mission ran churches, schools and clinics and trained Chinese priests and catechists.
He became a bishop in China and led the Irish mission there through the Japanese invasion and the civil war of the late 1930s and 1940s.
After the Communist takeover of 1949 the Irish missionaries faced restrictions, and Galvin was expelled from China in the early 1950s.
Contemporaries in Ireland saw Galvin and the China mission as heroes of the Catholic church, and their letters and talks raised vocations and money.
Chinese Communist authorities criticised the missionaries as agents of foreign influence, and this view shaped their expulsion.
Historians place the Maynooth missionaries in the wider history of Western missions, and they debate how far missionary work helped or hindered local communities.

notes.b: Mary Martin founded the Medical Missionaries of Mary, whose sisters combined nursing and medicine with mission work in Africa.
points: Mother Mary Martin founded the Medical Missionaries of Mary at Drogheda, County Louth, in 1937, to train women for medical and nursing work overseas.
The order trained doctors, nurses and midwives, and it set up hospitals and clinics in areas where few medical services existed.
Its sisters worked in Nigeria, and the order’s mission hospitals and nursing schools became central to its work there.
Martin directed the order’s expansion and the training of its members, and her leadership shaped its approach to medical work in the mission field.
Contemporary Irish Catholic opinion praised the order and its work, and the sisters were presented as models of the mission spirit.
Historians present the Medical Missionaries of Mary as a pioneer of women-led medical missions, and they ask how far medical work served colonial aims.

notes.h: Case study: the Holy Ghost mission to Nigeria, background
notes.b: The Holy Ghost Fathers, called Spiritans, were a French-founded congregation whose Irish members led much of the mission in south-eastern Nigeria.
points: The Holy Ghost Fathers (Spiritans) are a congregation founded in France, and Irish members of the congregation carried much of its work in Nigeria.
The Spiritans began work on the lower Niger in the 1880s, and they established their first mission at Onitsha, on the river.
The mission area was south-eastern Nigeria, where the Igbo people were the largest group, and the mission ran in what was then a British colony.
Bishop Joseph Shanahan, an Irish Spiritan, led the mission in the decades before the Second World War, and his work laid the foundations for schools and parishes.
By 1945 the mission had a network of parishes, schools and a few hospitals in the region, which the postwar expansion built on.

notes.b: Between 1945 and 1966 the mission grew into a large network of schools, hospitals and parishes, staffed by Irish missionaries and increasingly by Nigerians.
points: After 1945 the mission opened new parishes, schools, hospitals and training colleges across south-eastern Nigeria.
The number of Irish priests, brothers and sisters working in the mission rose in the 1950s, with recruits from Irish seminaries and novitiates.
Mission schools became the main route to education in the region, and the missions ran most primary and secondary schools.
Teacher training colleges prepared local teachers, which created a growing educated class in the region.
Hospitals and dispensaries provided medical care in rural areas where government services were few.
The Catholic population of the region grew strongly, and local vocations to the priesthood and religious life increased over the period.
Nigerians were trained as priests, teachers and nurses, and the mission gradually handed responsibility to local staff.

notes.h: Case study: the mission and the colonial state
notes.b: The mission depended on the colonial government for funding and cooperated with it, though the two sometimes disagreed over schooling and policy.
points: The colonial government paid grants towards mission schools under a grant-in-aid system, in return for inspection and standards.
The grants made education cheaper for the mission and for families, but they also tied the schools to government requirements.
Missions and colonial officials sometimes disagreed over curriculum, language and the role of religious teaching in schools.
Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960, and the mission adapted to a new state in which Nigerians held most public offices.
After independence the mission’s leadership passed increasingly to Nigerian priests and bishops, a process known as localisation.
Many of the educated Nigerians who served in the new state had passed through mission schools, which gave the mission a lasting role in the country’s élite.

notes.h: Case study: achievements, criticisms and the Biafran war
notes.b: The mission’s achievements in education and health can be set against criticisms of its cultural influence and against the damage of the Biafran war.
points: Achievements: the mission built schools, hospitals and churches, trained many local teachers and nurses, and helped create a Catholic church with Nigerian leadership.
Criticisms: mission education promoted Christian and Western values, and critics argued that it weakened local culture and languages.
Critics also said the mission was paternalistic, because Irish missionaries held the leadership long after local people were qualified for it.
On 30 May 1967 the eastern region declared itself the Republic of Biafra, and a civil war followed until January 1970.
During the war many mission stations, schools and hospitals were damaged, closed or abandoned, and missionaries were displaced.
Historians place the mission’s story in the transition from colonial rule to independence, and they judge it as both a source of education and a site of cultural change.

notes.b: The Irish missionary effort was presented at home as proof of Ireland’s global role, and it shaped how Irish Catholics saw themselves.
points: Irish Catholics saw the missions as a sign that Ireland was a nation with a mission of its own, not only a country that exported people.
The idea of an Irish spiritual empire combined Irish nationalism with the universal claims of the Catholic Church.
The missions raised money and vocations at home, and they linked Irish parishes to the lives of people overseas.
Later historians have questioned the empire idea, and they see it as a self-image that was closely tied to Irish Catholic identity and to the colonial world.

notes.b: Judgements on the missionaries turn on whether their schools and hospitals are seen as lasting contributions, or whether their cultural and colonial links are seen as the main legacy.
points: Achievement: the Holy Ghost mission built schools, hospitals and parishes that outlasted colonial rule and produced educated Nigerian leaders.
Limit: the mission was tied to the colonial state through grants, and it was slow to hand leadership to local clergy.
Contemporary view: Irish Catholics praised the missionaries as heroes of the faith, while some African critics questioned their paternalism and cultural impact.
Later view: historians stress both the practical contribution of missions to health and education and the cultural and political costs of their work.
